claims.text: Post-processing heat treatments can induce precipitation of secondary brittle intermetallic phases in a nominally single-phase high-entropy alloy.
Post-processing thermomechanical treatments can induce grain-boundary segregation in a nominally single-phase high-entropy alloy.
Secondary brittle phases or grain-boundary segregation act as stress concentrators.
These treatment-induced heterogeneities reduce toughness under demanding mechanical loads.
The initial alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
Thermal exposure and deformation trigger nucleation and growth of minute brittle intermetallic phases.
Thermal exposure and deformation can cause specific elements to segregate at grain boundaries.
Treatment-induced precipitates or grain-boundary segregation provide crack-initiation sites during mechanical loading.
Treated samples will have lower fracture energy than the untreated single-phase baseline.
Treated samples will have lower ductility than the untreated single-phase baseline.
Secondary precipitates or grain-boundary compositional inhomogeneities will correlate with reduced toughness.
The untreated, homogeneous single-phase baseline exhibits higher toughness and ductility than the treated material.
The proposed behavior applies under high mechanical stresses and significant loading rates.
The alloy maintains acceptable performance only under moderate loading, while loss of toughness becomes evident beyond those loading boundaries.
Precipitation kinetics and the magnitude of toughness loss depend on treatment temperature, treatment time, deformation degree, and alloy composition.
Order-disorder transitions may provide an alternative mechanism under similar conditions.
